name: Thymulin
lead: Thymulin, also called facteur thymique sérique (FTS) or serum thymic factor, is a nine-amino-acid peptide (pGlu-Ala-Lys-Ser-Gln-Gly-Gly-Ser-Asn) produced by the thymus and requiring zinc for biological activity [1][2]. It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 [1].

Research has concerned its role in T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation [1][3]. It is sold by some vendors as a research peptide in longevity circles, but no human trials of thymulin as a treatment were found, and it has no recognized appearance use.

paras: Thymulin is thought to help T-cell differentiation and to enhance T and NK cell activity. Its secretion follows a circadian rhythm and is linked to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis [1][4]. Levels decline with age, and it appears to dampen inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha in part by inhibiting NF-kB signaling [1].

Zinc dependence was shown in 1982, when metals were found to contribute to the activity of serum thymic factor [5]. A 1988 study found that serum thymulin activity fell in mildly zinc-deficient volunteers and recovered after zinc supplementation [6].

No studies found of thymulin as a treatment. The human data that exist concern zinc status and circulating thymulin activity [6]; an analog peptide has been examined in animal models of pain and neuroinflammation [1].
Thymulin is sold as a research peptide and is not an approved drug. Its link to looksmaxxing is indirect, through longevity and immune-support claims; no appearance outcomes have been studied.

timeline.event: Described as a serum thymic factor by Bach and colleagues.[1]

card.note: No clinical trials as a treatment; research-chemical sales.

quick.overview:
Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the thymus that needs zinc to be active. It has been studied for immune and neuroendocrine roles.

It is sold as a research peptide in longevity circles, but no trials of it as a treatment, and none for appearance, were found.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to promote T-cell maturation and temper inflammatory signaling, with activity depending on zinc binding.
quick.risks: No human safety trials of the peptide were found. It is not an approved drug and is sold unregulated.
